component.name: Mirdispo
component.summary: Share your Plasma desktop with Miracast displays

description.p: Mirdispo is a Plasma-native Wi-Fi Display sender. It finds compatible Miracast receivers, reports hardware and codec readiness, and guides the user through a screen-sharing session.

It supports Miracast over Wi-Fi Direct, Miracast over Infrastructure, and Chromecast. The casting itself is done by GNOME Network Displays, by Benjamin Berg, Christian Glombek and contributors, which is included with a small set of documented fixes.

screenshot.caption: Sharing the screen with a television

description.p: Casting works again on machines where it could not start at all: finding out whether the firewall was ready asked for a password behind a half-second deadline, so the prompt appeared and vanished before anyone could answer it.

The search for receivers now stops as soon as one is being reached, rather than once a picture is already arriving. It could never get that far, because the search swept the channels the two ends were trying to agree on.

The picture is sent at the rate the receiver was promised. About a sixth more frames were being sent than agreed, which the receiver threw away, and the bitrate meant for the agreed rate was spread over them.
Encoding happens on the graphics hardware where there is any, which leaves the picture unaffected by whatever else the machine is doing. It used to fall apart while its sender was being typed at.
A receiver offering a smaller picture at twice the rate is asked for that, which at a fixed bitrate is both smoother and sharper in anything that moves.
What a cast settled on is shown while it runs, and unfolding that line shows what it is doing from moment to moment.
Sound starts at seven tenths rather than full, which with a television's own volume was loud enough to reach for a remote.

Fixes sound dropping out and the picture stuttering, especially over Wi-Fi Direct. The encoder now keeps to its bitrate limit, which it never did: busy pictures came out in bursts no wireless link carries, and the backlog reached the sound.
Frames reach the receiver evenly again; the shorter delay in 3.6.0 made them arrive unevenly.
While a picture is being sent, Mirdispo pauses the search for receivers, which made the Wi-Fi radio scan other channels every 20 seconds.
A receiver whose network address could not be looked up at first, for instance just after it woke up, is found again instead of only over Wi-Fi Direct.

Receivers that can show full HD at 60 frames per second in the H.264 high profile now get it, twice as smooth as before at the same resolution. Mirdispo used to limit every receiver to the baseline profile.
The picture reaches the receiver about 70 ms sooner.
Receivers that take only one slice per picture get one, as they ask for.
Smoother and sharper motion. The picture no longer skips frames when you play video, drag windows or move the pointer, and it stays sharp while it moves, at the same resolution as before.
The sound on the receiver no longer stutters, and the picture and sound trail the desktop by less.

The desktop's sound now plays on the receiver along with the picture. Sound switches to the receiver when a cast starts and back to the previous output when it ends, without choosing a device in the sound settings.

A Wi-Fi Direct link that drops and comes back no longer uses up the retries for the rest of the session. Before, a long cast that lost its link twice, or one that needed a couple of attempts to connect, ended at the next drop instead of reconnecting.
Mirdispo finds its casting engine wherever it is installed, so installing from source into a prefix of your choice and running from a source checkout both work.
Mirdispo has an icon in the system tray. Closing the window keeps it running there, and the tray shows what is being shared, stops sharing, and quits.
Stopping screen sharing from the desktop, for instance with Plasma's screen sharing indicator, is now respected. Mirdispo no longer takes it for a lost connection and reconnects.

Fixes a working cast being reported as failed. The stream now reports when the receiver is getting a picture, and Mirdispo shows the session as active from that, also for receivers reached over the network rather than Wi-Fi Direct.
Closing Mirdispo while nothing is being cast now stops the casting engine too, so an update always takes effect the next time Mirdispo starts.

A Wi-Fi Direct handshake that the receiver has already given up on is retried after about 16 seconds instead of 45, now for every user and also in the Flatpak. It is noticed from the network interfaces rather than the system log, which only administrators can read.
In the Flatpak, the permission to share the screen is kept for the whole login session instead of being asked for again every time the application starts.

The casting engine no longer needs GTK or libadwaita, so installing Mirdispo pulls in far less. It registers on D-Bus under its own name and can no longer collide with GNOME Network Displays running on the same desktop. It also runs inside a Flatpak sandbox.

The application is now called Mirdispo and replaces the kde-network-displays package. The About page credits GNOME Network Displays, whose engine does the casting, and the Licence page says whose trademarks the protocol names are.
Diagnostics run from the command line find the casting backend, and any H.264 encoder the system has counts as a working video pipeline, not only OpenH264.
The licence page shows the licence itself and finds the source wherever the system keeps it, instead of naming paths that only exist on Debian and Ubuntu.
Removes code that nothing used any longer.
Uses software encoding again. Hardware encoding aborts inside the graphics driver when a cast is stopped, which was wrongly attributed to a fault in this project.
Picks the display mode from both ends: what the receiver accepts, what is being shared, and how much of it each mode would actually show.
Fixes the picture flashing on televisions: a receiver's television timings are used in preference to the computer monitor ones it also lists.
Streams the best mode a receiver says it supports, without preferring a sharper or a smoother picture on the viewer's behalf.
Chooses frames per second over pixels: a receiver offering 1080p at 30 Hz and 720p at 60 Hz now gets 60 Hz, so motion stops stuttering.
Records every display mode a receiver offers, so a poor choice can be told apart from a receiver that offers nothing better.
Sends the receiver a refresh rate it says it supports, instead of 30 Hz to everything. Motion should stop stuttering on receivers that take 60 Hz.
Uses the graphics chip to encode video again. Software encoding was forced after a crash whose real cause turned out to be a bug in this project, since fixed.
The About page is down to a name, a version and a line of credit, with the legal notices on a page of their own.
Each card's row now spans the card, so the action button sits in the same place whatever a receiver is called.
The layout test now measures the Plasma style the application actually runs under.
The Connect and Disconnect buttons now line up in one column whatever a receiver is called.
Credits the upstream project the streaming engine comes from, and describes what the application actually does today.

Completes the licence obligations for the GPL-3.0 code this builds on: the full licence text is shipped, the About page carries the copyright, warranty and modification notices, and every source file states its licence.
Strips creation metadata from the icons and uses documentation addresses in the demo, so nothing in the package records who built it.
Diagnostics now answers why casting would not work, instead of reporting radio facts nobody can act on.

Removes the Wi-Fi power saving switch. Its benefit was never demonstrated, it only took effect on the next Wi-Fi connection, and it applied to a route that is now the fallback. The diagnostics page still reports the setting.
Casts over your network when the receiver offers it, which connects in about a second and avoids Wi-Fi Direct channel negotiation entirely. Wi-Fi Direct stays the fallback.
Removes references to the hardware it was developed against, and third-party brand names from the demo, out of the shipped files.
Retries a failed group formation after two seconds instead of nine, since the receiver sends nothing to wait for in that case.
A lost handshake is retried as soon as wpa_supplicant reports it, instead of waiting out NetworkManager's 45 second timeout.
Stops asking which screen to share on every attempt, and never runs two stream helpers against the same receiver.
Keeps trying a receiver that ignores the handshake, standing off between attempts so the two sides stop talking over each other, and shows which attempt it is on.
A receiver that ignores the first handshake is retried immediately instead of waiting for the user to click again, which is what made connecting feel slow.
Diagnostics no longer print the kernel's name for the Wi-Fi adapter, and report the Wi-Fi channel rather than a frequency in megahertz.
Diagnostics rows now read alike: one short line each, and one icon family across the page.
The power saving control now reads "Power saving: ON" or "OFF" instead of leaving its state to an icon.
Wi-Fi power saving is now a switch beside Search again on the displays page, and the connection status is no longer printed twice.

Stops changing Wi-Fi settings behind a cast, since NetworkManager cannot apply power saving to a live connection anyway. The diagnostics page now offers the change as a button that verifies its own outcome and rolls back rather than risk the saved network password.
Handles the radio itself: Wi-Fi power saving is turned off for the duration of a cast and restored afterwards, and a refused handshake is retried before the user is told anything.
Checks whether Wi-Fi power saving is enabled, which makes the adapter sleep between beacons and drops casts mid-session, and names the command that turns it off.
Restarts the stream automatically when the Wi-Fi Direct link drops, so a brief radio glitch costs an interruption instead of the whole session.
Reports the Wi-Fi channel as diagnostic context instead of warning about a fault that testing did not confirm.
Reads the Wi-Fi Direct handshake state from NetworkManager, names the step it is on and the reason it failed, and warns when the adapter has to share its radio with the Wi-Fi network.
Shows each step of the Wi-Fi Direct handshake instead of a motionless "Connecting", and explains what to do when a receiver refuses the connection.
Connect now always starts the display that was clicked, and fixes two crashes: a use-after-free in receiver discovery and an unbounded loop when a Chromecast connection fails.
Fixes a crash when a cast is stopped, caused by unsafe PulseAudio teardown in the streaming backend.
Guarantees that the stream helper exits when a connection is cancelled before the screen chooser finishes.
Gives every cast attempt its own service instance, reports real start failures, and labels Miracast and Chromecast receivers correctly.
Uses software H.264 encoding to avoid a crash in a VA-API driver when a stream is stopped.
Initial production package with Kirigami UI, casting backend, diagnostics, and demo mode.
